text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The freedom of action that opponents of European currency union want to preserve won't be worth much unless Sweden has extremely strong state finances, Swedbank chief economist Hubert Fromlet says.
- Commercial bank S-E-Banken's Singapore office has been drawn into the investigation of irregular currency transactions undertaken at the bank's New York office.
- Finance magnate Erik Penser's stockbroking firm has taken over competitor Deriva Securities after the latter found itself in financial difficulties.

- Italian wines have taken market share from all other producer countries in Sweden's state alcohol retail monopoly. Sales of Italian wines increased by 11 percent over the first nine months of this year.

- Productivity in Swedish industry has increased by a record six percent per year over the period 1991 to 1995. Wages have not increased by nearly as much over the period, implying a sharp improvement in competitiveness over the period.

- Christina Jutterstrom, editor in chief of evening tabloid Expressen, has resigned after the journalists' union demanded a vote of no confidence in her. Expressen recently lost a hard-fought circulation battle against rival Aftonbladet.
- The number of murders in Sweden broke a downward trend last year. Statistics show that 179 people died a violent death in 1995, one for every 50,000 Swedes.
- A group of Swedish industrialists call for legislation against strikes. Wage negotiations must take place without the threat of industrial action hanging over employers.
- Labour minister Margareta Winberg criticised in the ruling Social Democratic party's parliamentary group over her impopular reform, now aborted, of unemployment benefits.
